Allow multiple start or end events when the description has distinct triggers or outcomes. Do not force all outcomes into one end.

Give every process and every expanded subProcess its own explicit start event and end event. A trigger that occurs after the main flow (for example later feedback or a return) is joined to the main flow by a gateway, or modeled as an event subprocess or a separate process.
Distinguish message tasks from message events: a task models performed work; an event models a message occurrence affecting flow.
Model every distinct activity, event, participant, decision, branch, loop, message and outcome stated in the description. Do not invent process facts.
Use an interrupting event-subprocess start when the parent scope stops; use non-interrupting only when the parent continues.

args.text: the description states that a condition occurring during the process (such as a disconnection) stops the process: model the occurrence as an intermediate catch event or boundary event that leads to a stop activity and an end event, not as a start event of a separate subprocess

trace.reason: Check whether error-driven guidelines already cover the start-event-of-subprocess mistake before classifying the relation.

result.rule: When the description states that a condition checked repeatedly during a monitoring activity (for example a disconnection or a measured figure crossing a limit) ends the process or triggers a consequence, and the description does not say that this condition can occur at any point of the process: Model the check as an exclusive gateway placed inside the monitoring loop, after the monitoring activity. Give the branch where the condition holds the consequence tasks in the order the description gives, ending at an end event (or returning to the loop merge if the description resumes monitoring). Give the other branch a flow back to the loop's merge point. Do not model the condition as an expanded subprocess with its own start event, and do not model it as a separate start event that is not triggered by the flow.

When The description says an external occurrence stops the whole running process at any point, with no return to the main flow.: Model that occurrence as an interrupting event subprocess inside the process, whose start event carries the occurrence's trigger type. Do not model it as a second process-level start event, and do not model it as a regular (non-event) subprocess placed in the main sequence flow.

When the description says the process ends only after a period of time elapses or a condition becomes true, following earlier activities: Model the waiting for the period to elapse or the condition to become true as an intermediate catch event (timer or conditional) placed before the end event on the sequence path. Do not model the wait as a task, because a task performs work and does not wait for an external time or condition.

When the description ends the process with a sentence in which a participant carries out a further described activity after the last stated step, and that activity is an action the flow still has to perform, not a received message or a state that is merely reached: Model that final performed activity as a task placed before the end event, in the performer's lane or pool when one is given. Close the flow with a plain end event whose name does not repeat the activity or its result. Do not use the end event to stand for the performed activity, and do not drop the activity from the model.

Title: OEE

Write a process, that collects relevant information from a machine, and calculated the Overall Equipment Efficiency (OEE).
If the OEE falls below a certain value/percentage, stop the machine and send an email to an engineer.
When the machine is restarted, continue measuring.
When the machine is disconnected, stop the process.
